title: Transport in Plants
description: The roles and positions of xylem and phloem in roots, stems and leaves, root hair cells and the pathway of water through the plant, the eosin stain investigation, and transpiration with the potometer practical for IGCSE Biology 0610.

notes.heading: Xylem and Phloem: the Two Transport Tissues (8.1.1)
notes.body:
📌 Definitions
• **Xylem** transports **water and mineral ions** — from the roots up the stem to the leaves — and also **gives the plant support**.
• **Phloem** transports **sucrose and amino acids** — from where they are made or stored to where they are needed.

🔑 What the examiner wants
Name the exact cargoes: xylem = water AND mineral ions; phloem = sucrose AND amino acids. 'Phloem transports food' is too vague for the mark — say which molecules. And remember xylem's second job: support — a frequent one-mark extra.

🔑 Direction
Water in the xylem moves UP (roots → stem → leaves) because the leaves are constantly losing water (transpiration — see the later note). Sucrose and amino acids in the phloem move to wherever the plant needs them — growing tips, roots, fruits, seeds.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Swapping the cargoes. Anchor it: Xylem = water ('xy' rhymes with 'dry' — it fixes thirst); Phloem = food molecules (sucrose, amino acids).

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Xylem: water + mineral ions, roots → leaves, plus support.
• Phloem: sucrose + amino acids, to wherever they are needed.

notes.heading: Where Xylem and Phloem Sit: Root, Stem and Leaf (8.1.2)
notes.body:
You must identify xylem and phloem in cross-sections of the root, stem and leaf of a **non-woody dicotyledonous** plant.

🔑 Root section
The **xylem is in the CENTRE** — often drawn as a cross or star shape — with **phloem in small patches between its arms**. A central column resists the pulling forces as the stem is tugged by wind.

🔑 Stem section
The vascular tissue is arranged as **vascular bundles in a ring** towards the outside of the stem. In each bundle, **xylem is on the INSIDE (towards the centre) and phloem on the OUTSIDE**.

🔑 Leaf section (midrib and veins)
In the midrib and veins, **xylem is on TOP and phloem is UNDERNEATH** — xylem delivers water upwards into the leaf, phloem carries sucrose away below.

💡 Worked Example
Given an unlabelled stem section: find the ring of bundles near the edge; within each bundle the tissue nearer the centre of the stem is xylem. Given a root section: look for the solid central core instead — that is xylem.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Applying the stem arrangement to the root. Root = central xylem; stem = ring of bundles with xylem inner and phloem outer; leaf vein = xylem above phloem.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Root: xylem central, phloem between its arms.
• Stem: bundles in a ring, xylem inside, phloem outside.
• Leaf: xylem on top, phloem below.

illustration.alt: Three diagrams showing xylem and phloem positions: a root cross-section with central star-shaped xylem and phloem between its arms, a stem cross-section with vascular bundles in a ring with xylem inside and phloem outside, and a leaf midrib with xylem above phloem.
illustration.caption: Root: xylem central. Stem: bundles in a ring, xylem inner, phloem outer. Leaf: xylem above phloem. Blue = xylem, orange = phloem.

notes.heading: Root Hair Cells (8.2.1–8.2.2)
notes.body:
📌 Identification
A **root hair cell** is a cell of the root's outer layer with a long, thin extension — the root hair — that grows out between the soil particles. You must be able to identify one on a diagram or micrograph: look for the finger-like projection on the outside of a young root, just behind the tip.

🔑 Function
Root hair cells **take up water and mineral ions from the soil**.

🔑 The adaptation
Each root carries thousands of root hairs, and together they give the root a **very large surface area** in contact with the soil. A large surface area **increases the uptake of water and mineral ions** — that cause-and-effect sentence is the marking point.

💡 Worked Example
'Explain how root hairs help a plant absorb water.' Frame the answer as: many root hairs → large surface area → more water (and mineral ions) taken up per unit time.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing root hairs with roots themselves: the hairs are microscopic extensions of single cells near the root tip, not small roots. They are also short-lived and constantly replaced as the root grows.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Root hair cell = epidermal cell with a long extension, found behind the root tip.
• Many hairs → large surface area → increased uptake of water and mineral ions.

notes.heading: The Pathway of Water Through the Plant (8.2.3)
notes.body:
📌 The pathway — learn the sequence
**root hair cells → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cells (of the leaf)**

🔑 Step by step
1. Water in the soil enters the **root hair cells**.
2. It passes across the **root cortex cells** towards the centre of the root.
3. It enters the **xylem**, which carries it up the stem to the leaves.
4. In the leaf, it moves from the xylem into the **mesophyll cells**, where it is used in photosynthesis or evaporates in transpiration.

🔑 What the examiner wants
Sequence questions ('put these in order' or 'describe the pathway') award a mark per correct link. Always start at the root hair cell and end at the mesophyll — and notice that water crosses the cortex BEFORE reaching the xylem, not after.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Sending water straight from the root hair into the xylem. The cortex cells sit between the epidermis and the central xylem, so water must cross them — omitting the cortex loses a mark.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Root hair → cortex → xylem → mesophyll.
• Xylem is the long-distance carrier between root and leaf.

notes.heading: Practical: Tracing the Water Pathway With a Stain (8.2.4)
notes.body:
🔑 The method
1. Cut the end off a leafy shoot (a **cut flower** or a stick of **celery** works well) and stand it in a solution of a coloured stain such as **eosin** (a red dye dissolved in water).
2. Leave it for several hours — longer if the light is bright.
3. Look at the leaves: the **veins** show the colour. Then cut thin sections of the stem and leaf stalk and look at them (a hand lens or microscope helps).

🔑 The result and conclusion
The stain appears **only in the xylem** — in the stem it marks the ring of vascular bundles, and in the leaf it marks the veins. Because the dye travelled with the water, this shows that **water moves through the plant in the xylem** and traces the pathway from stem to leaf.

🔑 Reliability details
Use several shoots and repeat; cut sections at several heights to show the dye rising over time. Cutting the shoot under water at the start keeps the xylem columns filled with water so uptake is not blocked by air.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Claiming the dye proves water moves in 'the veins' without naming the tissue. The vein contains BOTH xylem and phloem — the mark is for identifying **xylem** as the water-carrying tissue.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Eosin (or any coloured stain) + cut shoot → dye appears in xylem/veins.
• Conclusion: water travels in the xylem.

notes.heading: Transpiration (8.3.1–8.3.2)
notes.body:
📌 Definition
**Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the leaves** of a plant.

🔑 How it happens (8.3.2)
1. Water inside the leaf **evaporates from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells** into the **air spaces** of the spongy mesophyll.
2. The water vapour then **diffuses out of the leaf through the stomata**.
That two-step sequence — evaporate into the air spaces, diffuse out through the stomata — is exactly the phrasing the mark scheme rewards.

🔑 Why it matters
The constant loss of water from the leaves is what keeps water (and the mineral ions dissolved in it) moving up the xylem from the roots. Most of the water a plant absorbs is lost this way.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing that water is 'lost as liquid' or 'oozes out'. It leaves as water VAPOUR, by evaporation followed by diffusion. (How the loss at the leaf pulls the whole water column up — transpiration pull and cohesion — plus the effects of humidity and wilting, are Supplement objectives covered in the plant physiology topic.)

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Transpiration = loss of water vapour from leaves.
• Evaporation from mesophyll surfaces into air spaces → diffusion out through stomata.

notes.heading: Investigating Transpiration: Temperature and Wind (8.3.3)
notes.body:
🔑 The potometer practical
A **potometer** measures how fast a cut shoot takes up water — which stands in for the rate of transpiration, because nearly all the water taken up is lost from the leaves.
1. Cut a leafy shoot and fit it into the apparatus **under water**, sealing every joint so it is airtight.
2. Introduce a single **air bubble into the capillary tube**.
3. As the shoot takes up water, the bubble moves along the tube; measure the **distance moved in a measured time** and calculate the rate.
4. Repeat under changed conditions: a fan for different **wind speeds**, or water baths/rooms at different **temperatures**.

🔑 Describing the effects (Core level)
• **Increasing temperature → the transpiration rate increases** (evaporation from the mesophyll surfaces speeds up).
• **Increasing wind speed → the transpiration rate increases** (moving air carries the escaped water vapour away, so diffusion out of the leaf stays fast).

🔑 Validity
Change ONE factor at a time and keep the other constant; use the same shoot; let the apparatus settle before each set of readings; reset the bubble between runs.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying the potometer 'measures transpiration directly'. It measures water UPTAKE by the shoot — an excellent approximation, but a small amount of the water is used by the plant (e.g. in photosynthesis) rather than transpired.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Potometer: bubble distance ÷ time = rate of water uptake.
• More heat → faster transpiration; more wind → faster transpiration.

flashcards.definition: The tissue that transports water and mineral ions from the roots up to the leaves, and also supports the plant.
flashcards.example: In a root section, xylem is the central tissue; in a stem it is on the inside of each vascular bundle.

flashcards.definition: The tissue that transports sucrose and amino acids from where they are made or stored to where they are needed.
flashcards.example: Sucrose made in the leaves travels in the phloem to growing fruits and roots.

flashcards.definition: In a non-woody dicot stem, the bundles of xylem and phloem arranged in a ring — xylem on the inside, phloem on the outside.
flashcards.example: An eosin stain experiment colours the ring of bundles in the stem, showing the xylem.

flashcards.definition: A cell of the root's outer layer with a long extension between soil particles; it takes up water and mineral ions.
flashcards.example: Thousands of root hairs give the root a very large surface area for uptake.

flashcards.term: Large surface area of root hairs
flashcards.definition: The many microscopic hairs hugely increase the area in contact with the soil, increasing the uptake of water and mineral ions.
flashcards.example: Removing root hairs (e.g. by rough transplanting) makes a plant wilt until they regrow.

flashcards.definition: Root hair cells → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cells of the leaf.
flashcards.example: Water absorbed by a root hair crosses the cortex before entering the xylem that carries it to the leaf.

flashcards.definition: A cut shoot (or celery/flower) stood in red eosin solution: after several hours the dye is seen in the xylem and leaf veins, showing the pathway of water.
flashcards.example: Stem sections show a red ring of vascular bundles; leaf sections show red veins.

flashcards.definition: The loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant.
flashcards.example: Water evaporates from mesophyll cell surfaces into the air spaces, then diffuses out through the stomata.

flashcards.definition: Pores, mostly on the lower epidermis of the leaf, through which water vapour diffuses out of the leaf.
flashcards.example: Open stomata allow gas exchange for photosynthesis but also let water vapour escape.

flashcards.definition: The leaf cells from whose surfaces water evaporates into the air spaces during transpiration.
flashcards.example: Moist spongy mesophyll walls keep the leaf's air spaces humid until the vapour diffuses out.

flashcards.definition: Apparatus that measures the rate of water uptake by a cut shoot by tracking an air bubble along a capillary tube; used to investigate transpiration.
flashcards.example: Rate = distance the bubble moves ÷ time, compared across temperatures or wind speeds.

flashcards.term: Effect of temperature and wind on transpiration
flashcards.definition: Increasing temperature increases the transpiration rate, and increasing wind speed increases the transpiration rate.
flashcards.example: A potometer bubble moves fastest on a warm, windy day.

choices: Water and mineral ions
Sucrose and amino acids
Oxygen and carbon dioxide
Starch and cellulose
questions.explanation: Xylem carries water and mineral ions from the roots to the leaves (and supports the plant). Sucrose and amino acids travel in the phloem — swapping the two cargoes is the classic error.

choices: Water from the soil
Mineral ions from the roots
Sucrose and amino acids
Oxygen for respiration
questions.explanation: Phloem carries sucrose and amino acids to the parts of the plant that need them. Water and mineral ions are xylem's cargo, and naming the molecules earns the mark where 'food' would not.

questions.stem: In a cross-section of a non-woody dicotyledonous STEM, where are the xylem and phloem found?
choices: Scattered randomly through the stem
In vascular bundles arranged in a ring, with xylem on the inside and phloem on the outside
In a single solid block in the very centre
Only in the epidermis
questions.explanation: In the stem the vascular tissue forms bundles in a ring near the outside; within each bundle the xylem faces the centre and the phloem faces outward. A central core of xylem describes the ROOT, not the stem.

questions.stem: In a cross-section of a dicotyledonous ROOT, where is the xylem?
choices: In a ring of bundles near the outside
In the root hairs
In the cortex
In the centre of the root
questions.explanation: Root xylem forms a central (often star- or cross-shaped) core with phloem in patches between its arms — an arrangement that resists pulling forces. The ring-of-bundles arrangement belongs to the stem.

questions.stem: What is the function of a root hair cell?
choices: Photosynthesis in the root
Taking up water and mineral ions from the soil
Anchoring the plant firmly in the ground
Producing sucrose for the phloem
questions.explanation: Root hair cells absorb water and mineral ions from the soil. Roots are underground (no light, no chlorophyll, so no photosynthesis), and anchorage is done by the root system as a whole, not the hairs.

questions.stem: Why do the thousands of root hairs on a young root increase the uptake of water and mineral ions?
choices: They contain chlorophyll to power the uptake
They secrete enzymes into the soil
They are dead cells with no contents
They give the root a very large surface area in contact with the soil
questions.explanation: Each hair is a tiny extension of a single cell; thousands of them multiply the surface area touching soil water, so more water and mineral ions can be taken up at once. Root hairs are living cells and contain no chlorophyll.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly gives the pathway of water through a plant?
choices: Root hair cells → root cortex cells → xylem → mesophyll cells
Xylem → root cortex cells → root hair cells → mesophyll cells
Mesophyll cells → xylem → root cortex cells → root hair cells
Root hair cells → xylem → root cortex cells → mesophyll cells
questions.explanation: Water enters the root hairs, crosses the cortex, reaches the central xylem, and is carried up to the leaf mesophyll. The cortex lies between the epidermis and the xylem, so it must come before the xylem in the sequence.

questions.stem: A stick of celery is stood in red eosin solution for several hours, then thin sections of the stalk are cut. What is observed, and what does it show?
choices: Every tissue is stained red — water moves through all cells equally
Only the phloem is stained — water moves in the phloem
The dye is seen in the xylem (and the leaf veins) — showing that water moves through the plant in the xylem
Only the outer epidermis is stained — water travels up the outside of the stem
questions.explanation: The red dye travels dissolved in the water, so it marks the exact tissue the water moves through: the xylem in the stem bundles and the veins of the leaf. This is the standard Core investigation of the pathway of water.

choices: The uptake of water by the roots
The movement of sucrose in the phloem
The evaporation of water from wet soil
The loss of water vapour from the leaves
questions.explanation: Transpiration is defined as the loss of water vapour from a plant's leaves. Water uptake by roots happens before it, and evaporation from soil is not part of the plant at all.

questions.stem: How does water leave the leaf during transpiration?
choices: It evaporates from the mesophyll cell surfaces into the air spaces, then diffuses out through the stomata
It is pumped out of the leaf by the guard cells
It seeps as liquid through the waxy cuticle
It moves by active transport through the upper epidermis
questions.explanation: The two steps are: evaporation from the moist surfaces of mesophyll cells into the leaf's air spaces, then diffusion of the water vapour out through the stomata. The waxy cuticle is waterproof, and no pumping or active transport is involved.

questions.stem: What does a potometer actually measure?
choices: The exact rate of transpiration from the leaves
The rate of photosynthesis in the shoot
The rate of water uptake by the cut shoot, which approximates the transpiration rate
The rate of mineral ion absorption
questions.explanation: The moving bubble tracks the water taken up by the shoot. Because nearly all of that water is lost as vapour from the leaves, uptake closely approximates transpiration — but a little water is used by the plant, so it is not a direct measurement.

questions.stem: A potometer experiment is repeated at a higher temperature, with all other conditions kept the same. What happens to the movement of the air bubble?
choices: It moves more slowly
It moves faster — the transpiration rate increases as temperature increases
It does not move at all
It moves backwards towards the shoot
questions.explanation: Higher temperature speeds up evaporation of water from the mesophyll surfaces, so the transpiration rate rises, the shoot takes up water faster, and the bubble travels further in the same time.

questions.stem: How does increasing the wind speed around a leafy shoot affect the rate of transpiration?
choices: It decreases the rate
It has no effect on the rate
It increases the rate
It stops transpiration completely
questions.explanation: Moving air carries away the water vapour that has diffused out of the stomata, so diffusion out of the leaf stays fast and the transpiration rate increases. In a potometer this shows up as the bubble moving faster.

questions.stem: When setting up a potometer, the shoot is cut under water and every joint is sealed to be airtight. Why are these steps necessary?
choices: To keep the leaves cool during the experiment
To stop air entering the xylem, and to make sure the bubble's movement reflects water taken up by the shoot only
To prevent any water evaporating from the leaves
To allow the shoot to photosynthesise faster
questions.explanation: Cutting under water keeps air out of the xylem so water uptake continues, and airtight seals mean no water can enter or leave the apparatus except through the shoot — so the bubble movement genuinely tracks the shoot's water uptake.

questions.stem: Which row correctly matches a tissue with what it transports and where it is found?
choices: Xylem — transports water and mineral ions — central in a root section
Phloem — transports water — on the outside of each stem bundle
Xylem — transports sucrose — on top in a leaf vein
Phloem — transports mineral ions — between the arms of the root xylem
questions.explanation: Xylem carries water and mineral ions and sits centrally in the root. The other rows mix the cargoes up: phloem carries sucrose and amino acids (not water or mineral ions), and in a leaf vein xylem is on top but carries water, not sucrose.
